title: Weekly carboplatin + paclitaxel with radiotherapy
purpose: Chemotherapy is given alongside radiotherapy to treat stage III non-small-cell lung cancer when cisplatin is unsuitable. Your team explains the treatment aim and choices.

agents.name: Paclitaxel
agents.explanation: Paclitaxel stabilises structures needed for cell division. It can also affect nerves, blood cells and healthy tissues. Premedicines help reduce infusion reactions.
agents.watch: Report numbness, tingling, muscle/joint pain or new breathing symptoms.

agents.name: Carboplatin
agents.explanation: Carboplatin forms links in DNA that interfere with cell copying. Its dose uses kidney filtration and target exposure(AUC), not a fixed number of milligrams.
agents.watch: Report fever, unusual bleeding, vomiting or allergy symptoms.

phases.label: Seven weekly chemotherapy treatments
phases.detail: Both medicines are given by drip once every 7 days for seven weeks, alongside a separate radiotherapy course. The plan may change for side effects or test results. Further chemotherapy after radiotherapy is a separate decision.

phases.label: Radiation course
phases.detail: Radiation is given during the chemotherapy course. Its dose, number of fractions and precise timing are prescribed by radiation oncology. A chemotherapy delay does not automatically stop radiation.

phases.label: After chemoradiation
phases.detail: Your team reviews recovery and response. NCCP describes optional separate two-cycle carboplatin/paclitaxel consolidation under00304; it is not automatically included and any next treatment needs a separate prescription.

timeline.label: Paclitaxel then carboplatin
timeline.text: One weekly chemotherapy visit after blood tests and premedicines.

timeline.label: Symptoms and separate RT plan
timeline.text: Continue the written radiation and support plan. Symptoms may occur on any day; this is not a radiation-fraction calendar.

day_groups.title: Weekly treatment day
day_groups.body: Blood results and symptoms are reviewed. Paclitaxel comes first, followed by carboplatin.
day_groups.action: Tell staff immediately about flushing, breathing trouble, pain or swelling during infusion.

day_groups.title: Support at home
day_groups.body: Use the anti-sickness medicines prescribed for these days. Radiation visits may continue on their own schedule.
day_groups.action: Call for fever, poor intake, vomiting or new breathing symptoms.

day_groups.title: Before the next weekly dose
day_groups.body: Keep track of swallowing, fatigue, numbness and muscle/joint symptoms. Arrange the next weekly blood tests.
day_groups.action: Report problems before the next dose; do not wait if acutely unwell.

support.title: Weekly medicines before treatment
support.text: Paclitaxel needs premedicines to reduce allergic reactions. The first week and later weeks can differ. Your team also provides anti-sickness medicines for carboplatin; do not double up steroid doses.

support.title: Eating, swallowing and breathing
support.text: Chest radiation can make swallowing sore. Ask early for pain relief and nutrition support. New breathlessness, cough or inability to drink needs urgent advice, even after the course finishes.

support.title: Nerves and aches
support.text: Tell the team about numbness, tingling or muscle/joint pain before each weekly visit. Follow the agreed pain-relief plan and check before starting medicines or supplements.

questions.q: Which drugs and routes are prescribed for me?
questions.a: Confirm the exact drug names, routes and interval against your written prescription. The team must explain any change from this reference plan.

questions.q: How do my radiation appointments fit around chemotherapy?
questions.a: Radiation has its own calendar. Ask for the combined plan and whom to contact if a chemotherapy or radiation visit changes.

questions.q: Which blood tests are required before the next dose?
questions.a: Use the checks table as a prompt. Your team confirms which tests are needed, where they are done and who reviews the results before treatment.

questions.q: Who do I call during the day and overnight?
questions.a: Ask the team to replace the example numbers on your card with the correct daytime, overnight and backup contact routes before you leave.

questions.q: When will recovery and response be reviewed?
questions.a: Agree the follow-up appointments and any scans with your team. This regimen does not set a universal scan or tumour-marker timetable.

sources.title: Choy et al.1998 · phase II weekly chemoradiation

context_label: Stage III non-small-cell lung cancer · concurrent chemoradiation
schedule_summary: Both medicines are given by drip once every 7 days for seven weeks, alongside a separate radiotherapy course. The plan may change for side effects or test results. Further chemotherapy after radiotherapy is a separate decision.
administration_text: Paclitaxel is infused first over one hour, then carboplatin over 30 minutes, plus checks and premedicines. The consultant may prescribe a lower paclitaxel dose. RT appointments are separate and are not counted as chemotherapy doses.
monitoring_summary: Blood count, kidney and liver tests before treatment. Measured kidney filtration is preferred, or a verified estimate. Hearing and nerve assessment if clinically indicated. Blood count with differential, kidney and liver tests every week. Check nerve symptoms if indicated. If GFR is calculated, creatinine must be within 48 hours of carboplatin. After treatment, your team checks recovery, persistent symptoms and response. Scan type/timing and any useful tumour-marker testing are individual decisions; this regimen does not specify a universal scan or marker timetable.
urgent_extra: Call oncology immediately for fever, shaking chills, sudden illness, new breathlessness, uncontrolled vomiting, inability to swallow fluids, much less urine or unusual bleeding. Severe breathing difficulty, chest pain, collapse or heavy bleeding needs emergency care. Tell staff immediately about infusion pain, swelling or allergy symptoms.
consent_support: Discuss serious infection/sepsis and possible hospital admission, bleeding, infusion reactions, lung inflammation, painful swallowing/dehydration, fatigue, fertility, hair loss and individual material risks. Paclitaxel neuropathy may persist; discuss muscle/joint pain, renal dose checks and late respiratory symptoms after chest radiation. Radiotherapy needs its own informed-consent discussion; chemotherapy consent does not replace it.

chronology_notes.title: Relative schedule, not personal dates
chronology_notes.text: Both medicines are given by drip once every 7 days for seven weeks, alongside a separate radiotherapy course. The plan may change for side effects or test results. Further chemotherapy after radiotherapy is a separate decision.

chronology_notes.title: Radiation is a separate schedule
chronology_notes.text: Chemotherapy Day 1/Day 2/Day 3 or weekly counts are not radiation fractions. The radiation oncology team supplies the exact RT timetable.

chronology_notes.title: No fixed symptom day
chronology_notes.text: Sickness, fatigue, low counts, swallowing problems or breathing symptoms can occur between visits and after treatment. Do not wait for a calendar window to seek advice.

timeline_note: Reference cycle without patient dates. RT visits and dose are separately prescribed; the symptom band is not a nadir prediction.
safety_note: Call oncology immediately for fever, shaking chills, sudden illness, new breathlessness, uncontrolled vomiting, inability to swallow fluids, much less urine or unusual bleeding. Severe breathing difficulty, chest pain, collapse or heavy bleeding needs emergency care. Tell staff immediately about infusion pain, swelling or allergy symptoms.
passport_visit_note: Bring your contact card and medication list. Record each chemotherapy treatment and separately confirm the radiation appointments.
anatomy: Report numbness, tingling, weakness or difficulty with everyday tasks before treatment.
Tell the team if swallowing becomes painful. Inability to drink needs urgent advice.
New breathlessness or worsening cough needs urgent review, including after treatment ends.
Use prescribed anti-sickness treatment; call for uncontrolled vomiting or dehydration.
Kidney tests help calculate the dose. Report reduced urine or dehydration.
Call for fever or bleeding. Report muscle/joint pain and any infusion-site swelling.

monitoring_schedule.title: My tests and treatment checks
monitoring_schedule.note: Required safety tests are distinct from team-agreed imaging and follow-up; no universal tumour-marker interval is specified.

sections.title: Confirm your plan
sections.text: Paclitaxel is infused first over one hour, then carboplatin over 30 minutes, plus checks and premedicines. The consultant may prescribe a lower paclitaxel dose. RT appointments are separate and are not counted as chemotherapy doses.

sections.title: Keep the contact card
sections.text: The team supplies the daytime and out-of-hours numbers. Keep the card with you and show it when seeking medical care.

sections.title: Two linked treatment teams
sections.text: Confirm which team to contact for radiation or chemotherapy changes. Report swallowing problems early and ask about transport, nutrition and fatigue support.

evidence.title: Why chemotherapy and radiotherapy are combined
evidence.intro: Studies support combining systemic treatment with radiation in the relevant lung-cancer setting.
evidence.interpretation: The evidence comes from specific treatment schedules and patient groups. Your team explains how it applies to your situation; study averages cannot predict an individual outcome.

patient_summary.purpose: Chemotherapy and radiation treat stage III non-small-cell lung cancer when cisplatin is unsuitable. Your team explains your treatment aim and options.
patient_summary.schedule: Paclitaxel then carboplatin by drip once every 7 days for seven weeks, alongside separately scheduled radiotherapy. Test results or side effects may change treatment. Any treatment after this course needs a separate decision and prescription.

phases.title: Chemotherapy
phases.text: Both drugs at each weekly visit, after blood tests, symptom review and premedicines.

phases.title: Radiotherapy
phases.text: The radiation team sets the dose and appointments. A chemotherapy delay does not automatically stop radiation.

phases.title: After treatment
phases.text: Your team reviews recovery, persistent symptoms and response. Scan or marker timing is individual.

Bring your medicine list and daytime / overnight contact numbers.

monitoring.when: Measured GFR preferred; otherwise verified estimate
Weekly; creatinine within 48 hours for calculated GFR

cycle_expectations: Use the prescribed anti-sickness medicines; report numbness, swallowing pain, fatigue or muscle and joint symptoms before treatment.
Fever, new breathlessness, uncontrolled vomiting or inability to drink needs urgent advice, including after the course ends.
